 We’ve seen it before: Common themes to expect on and before Election Day
 Oct 28, 2026 | 2026 Rapid Research Blog , Rapid Research Blog , Research 
 What to Expect When We’re Electing 
 This blog post was written by the Election Rumor Research team at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public and crossposted on the CIP’s Election Rumor Rundown Substack newsletter. 
 Since 2020, we have observed a steady drumbeat of election rumors each election cycle. They have become common enough that election administrators now regularly prepare for and respond to election rumors as a core part of their job.
 Through multiple cycles of rapid response work, our research team has identified a substantial number of election rumors — and mapped those rumors to 35 million tweets — that we have analyzed using systematic, academic methods. In reviewing these datasets, we have seen how the same claims and themes occur repeatedly to the point that the rumors have become surprisingly predictable, enough so that we made a bingo card based on the most common claims we’ve observed. We have drafted a full report detailing the methods and findings of this analysis which we will link to as soon as it is available.
 Here, we outline some of the major themes — or what we term “tropes” — emerging from our analysis, and highlight claims we expect to resurface in the lead up to and on election day. We also draw and integrate insights from a previous explainer we wrote in 2024 about anticipated election rumors.
 A Brief Note on Our Framework 
 First, let’s take a high-level look at the framework presented in greater detail in our forthcoming full article, “New Election, Same Old Story: How Tropes Form a Grammar of Election Rumors.” Figure 1 shows a subset of the most commonly occurring themes, grouped into three concentric rings. The outer ring shows the claims themselves. We view these claims as the “building blocks” of modern election rumors. Typically the rumors that we document in our work involve several of these themes combined together, like rumor-building lego blocks. For example, we recently wrote a post analyzing rumors surrounding a video of election workers in a ballot tabulation center in Maricopa County, Arizona . That rumor focused on Arizona, a swing state , involved allegations of machine manipulation by election workers , and occurred late at night . Each of these bolded terms are elements we have seen before, and are often used as the building blocks of “novel” rumors that add something slightly new to a tired, old script.
 Figure 1: Wheel chart showing meta categories in the inner circle, such as Objects or Actors; the middle circle shows meso categories, such as Suspicious Statistics or Villains; and the outer circle shows micro tropes (themes in this post), such as Improbable Results or Election Officials. These “micro tropes” are what we discuss in this blog post as claims and themes. What is displayed in this chart is not a complete list of the themes we have documented. 
 Rumors to Expect in the Lead-Up to Election Day 
 Perhaps the most useful aspect of the framework visualized in Figure 1 is that it is a tool for predicting future rumors. With Election Day less than a week away, we can use our data to help election officials, voters, and online audiences anticipate rumors that we are likely to see before, during, and after the election. Below, we cover some of the most common claims emerging from our framework that we have seen in the past, are already seeing, and are likely to see in the coming weeks.
 Rumors About “Dirty” Voter Rolls and Illegitimate Registrations 
 We have already covered some of the rumors that emerge from doubt surrounding the accuracy of voter rolls, and we expect to continue to see claims that emerge from this doubt up to, on, and after Election Day.  
 Non-citizen voting: Most notable is the case of rumors alleging non-citizens are voting en masse, usually conspiratorially framed as part of a larger Democratic-led plan to “import” non-citizens across the southern border and have them dilute the votes of American citizens. We have already highlighted how federal law enforcement agencies have participated in catalyzing rumors that resonate with this false narrative, and expect to continue to see these claims spread online. We’ve also documented non-citizen voting rumors in California and a flurry of federal charges outlined in press releases by the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security around the country.
 Dead voters: Rumors alleging that people are voting using the names of dead people are also very common. Most commonly, rumors of this type involve misinterpretations of publicly available voter roll data , often due to default values in registration databases being the year 1900. We also see reports of people who have recently died receiving mail-in ballots due to delays in processing their deaths, leading to rumors about their ballots becoming a vector for fraud.
 Multiple people, same address:  We may see rumors alleging that multiple ballots sent to a single address reflect an illegal vote harvesting operation. Oftentimes, people who do not have a consistent home register to vote using a P.O. box or a shelter, which is the most common reason multiple people are registered at a single address. We saw such a case during the California primary when an infamous conservative vlogger incited false rumors about many voters registered at a UPS store in San Diego, which turned out to be part of a large apartment complex.
 In-Person and Mail-In Voting Rumors 
 The early voting period has already begun in several states and as voters begin voting we expect to see rumors emerging around anything that might go wrong during the process. The majority of in-person voters do not vote early, so the quantity of rumors is likely to be smaller than on Election Day, but some of the rumors are similar.
 Voting Machine Rumors 
 Rumors surrounding voting machines occur every election cycle and tend to peak on Election Day — we’ve written an in-depth explainer about them before. However, we also see some machine-related rumors during early voting for states that use electronic voting machines. 
 Machines flipping votes: We anticipate, and have already begun to see , rumors about machines flipping votes away from the candidate a voter is trying to select. Historically, these types of rumors emerge from poorly designed or malfunctioning interfaces (and occasionally user error) but are often misleadingly framed as intentional attempts to switch votes instead of rare errors with remedies.  
 Corrupt Machines: We also anticipate seeing rumors suggesting that voting machines are corrupted from the get-go, claiming that a nefarious entity is manipulating the final count of the machines. We’ve already seen misleading claims that machines with foreign parts are a national security risk — setting the rhetorical ground for executive action. There are strict guidelines around testing machines prior to use and ensuring that the machines that are used have auditable records for every vote cast. Dominion Voting Systems famously won over a $1 billion lawsuit based on unfounded claims of their machines being corrupted. 
 Mail-In Voting 
 Mail-in voting has been a contentious issue since 2020, and recent changes to U.S. Postal Service postmarking policies alongside attempts to limit mail-in voting via executive orders have continued to create fertile ground for rumoring.  
 Dumped/destroyed/delayed/missing ballots: Some of the most common rumors surrounding mail-in ballots focus on ballots being mishandled in some way, including being thrown away or dumped in a ditch, mysteriously gone missing, destroyed, or otherwise delayed in their delivery. There are real instances of mail being thrown away , but it is usually unrelated to any attempt to disenfranchise voters. Instead, it may be related to attempts to lighten workload. Bad, but more about mail in general than ballots in particular. Similarly, cases of delayed or missing ballots are usually a result of administrative or procedural issues, not intentional attempts to hide mail. Occasionally ballots are stolen, along with other mail, from mailboxes and then discarded by the thieves, but these cases are very rare, not likely to be politically motivated, and are typically remedied by election officials who can alert voters and issue new ballots. 
 Ballots arriving late or after deadline: Historically we have seen many rumors and claims alleging that election workers illegally count ballots received after Election Day. Many states allow for the counting of late-arriving ballots as long as they are postmarked prior to Election Day. However, recent rule changes to when USPS postmarks mail , specifically moving postmarking from local to regional facilities, makes it so that mail is likely to be postmarked later, resulting in larger numbers of ballots whose postmarks are too late to be counted. We anticipate this being fertile ground for uncertainty, rumoring, and sincere grievance about voter disenfranchisement. 
 Ballot materials mailed to the wrong person or multiple ballots received by the same person: We expect to see rumors, usually alongside photos, of people who received multiple ballots or the ballot of the wrong person — in fact we’ve already seen some of these cases which have been remedied . Mailing mistakes do happen, this type of error is not evidence of fraud and there are safeguards in place to ensure that each person is only able to have one vote counted. We strongly recommend that people don’t try to test this system, because intentionally voting twice is both illegal and likely to be discovered. 
 Typos and poorly printed ballots : Another common rumor type we see are those that misleadingly suggest that poorly printed ballots or ballots with typos are intentionally disseminated to disenfranchise voters . As with many of the examples we name above, mistakes can happen when conducting an election at such a large scale. Those types of mistakes are typically not intentional, and voters can request a new ballot if their original ballot has errors on it. 
 Voter suppression and armed monitoring of drop boxes: We expect to see reports, and possibly real incidents, of people watching ballot drop boxes, sometimes armed or in tactical gear, photographing voters or following them. Threats, intimidation and coercion are illegal under the federal Voting Rights Act. Drop boxes are secure, often under video surveillance, and voters can use them with confidence. This category includes seeing ICE at the polls. It is important to recognize that false rumors of ICE at polling centers has the potential to suppress votes for those who may become afraid to show up for fear of intimidation or harassment, so reporting should be careful to ensure that there is a credible threat before sharing unverified information. Some states are taking proactive measures to assuage anxiety; Washington State has already offered plainclothes, unarmed members of the National Guard to protect drop boxes.  
 Ballot harvesting: We expect to see rumors, often accompanied with ambiguous photos or videos, of people dropping off several ballots at once, and misleadingly alleging that those people are illegally voting . In reality, many states explicitly allow a third party to return a completed ballot, and in many cases the person is returning ballots for family members or for voters who can’t easily get to a drop box. A video of someone depositing multiple ballots is not evidence of fraud. Every ballot still goes through signature verification and voter record checks, and each voter can have only one ballot counted.  
 Election Day 
 On Election Day we anticipate seeing many rumors similar to the ones above as well as several that are unique to Election Day (and the days after). We’ve written about these before as well. 
 Machine glitches, malfunctions, or breakdowns: In some cases, electronic voting machines and/or tabulators malfunction or cease to work , leading to online rumors surrounding the issue. Glitches and malfunctions often result in delays and increased periods of uncertainty that is fertile ground for rumors, especially in places that already expect to see fraud. Conspiratorial rumoring often misleadingly frames these issues as “intentional errors” that are used to disenfranchise voters by either preventing them from voting, manipulating their vote, or forcing them to vote via a perceived untrustworthy alternative, such as putting a ballot in a box to be handcounted later. 
 Bomb threats and polling center closures: We also anticipate seeing reports of bomb threats or other disruptions that temporarily close or otherwise impact polling places. In past elections, most threats have been hoaxes, but they may need investigation which can cause delays during voting. Election officials have contingency plans in such scenarios, which includes relocating to a different site or extending voting hours. Online activists and other communicators should be careful about amplifying these rumors on (and before) Election Day, because they can scare voters, potentially leading to voter suppression.  
 Day-of errors, delays, and long lines: We anticipate seeing rumors about long lines, equipment malfunctions, polling centers opening late, or other anomalies misleadingly framed as deliberate suppression or fraud. In some cases, long lines are downstream of policies that make it harder to vote in some areas, and frustration is understandable — though reports of long lines can suppress votes. In other cases, the issues result from accidental equipment errors. Most are resolved quickly. Back-up procedures, such as paper ballots or emergency ballot boxes, allow people to still vote when equipment fails. In the case of long lines and other delays, voters already in line are able to vote, and there are sometimes alternative voting locations people can go to if one is very far behind schedule. 
 “Suspicious” remedies to voting issues: We also anticipate seeing misleading rumors alleging that remedies for Election Day errors or malfunctions are untrustworthy and are actually a vector of fraud . For example, voters in the past have been asked to put ballots in a secure box for counting offsite when tabulators are unable to count their ballot. Different issues have different remedies, but in many cases they are often unfamiliar to impacted voters, creating fertile ground for rumoring, especially if voters are primed via partisan media to see fraud in anything they don’t recognize. 
 Election Night and Beyond 
 Biased early media calls: Historically we have seen claims that media outlets call races early to influence voters or favor one side in order to sow mistrust in election results. It is important to recognize that media projections are estimates based on partial results and are not official results. In reality, results only become official once they are certified which is typically weeks after Election Day. 
 Statistically impossible results and vote dumps: Vote counting results are often reported in batches, so totals can shift sharply when a large batch, such as mail ballots or results from a big county, are released. When these spikes are visualized in graphs, they show sharp increases and plateaus in vote counts that to many audiences looks suspicious unless they know how counts are reported. This results in misleading rumors that the sudden jumps in vote totals, frequently called “vote dumps,” are evidence of fraud — as we saw happen earlier this year in the California mayoral primary . 
 Late-night manipulation, suspicious vehicles, and containers of ballots: In the past, we have often seen rumors involving ambiguous photos or videos of unmarked vehicles or unfamiliar containers presented as evidence of manipulation or alleged fraud . In some cases, people assume there are ballots in a box that contains something else, such as camera equipment, while in others ballots may be transferred to another location for counting. In the cases where ballots are being moved, there are chain-of-custody procedures that typically include sealed containers, logs, and bipartisan teams.  
 Slow vote counting: We expect to see rumors misleadingly alleging that “slow counting” means that results are intentionally being slowed down so they can be manipulated. Some states like California are known for slower counting due to statewide mail-in voting and provisions for people to correct problems with their signature verification. In reality, counting takes time, especially for mail ballots, which have signatures and postmarks verified before they can be tabulated. Additionally, some states don’t allow processing to begin until Election Day, and mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day may still arrive and be counted for days afterward. None of this is evidence of fraud. 
 Hacked machines: We anticipate seeing rumors alleging that voting machines were hacked or otherwise accessed without authorization. Usually rumors of this type involve allegations of machines being connected to the internet, a USB being inserted into a machine, fears of foreign interference, or concerns they are being manipulated by Starlink systems . Election machines undergo certifications to ensure they are secure, and there is no current evidence to suggest they are vulnerable to hacking.  
 Beyond Election Day 
 Elections are not guaranteed to be called on election night, creating an extended period of uncertainty during which rumors spread. Many of the rumor types we already outlined are likely to continue to spread in the days after the election.  
 This election cycle, there is uncertainty surrounding how the current administration may react should they lose the election, which creates even more fertile ground for rumoring. In the past, rumors surrounding slow counting and the statistics of vote counts lasted long after Election Day. Among those rumors, claims of machine manipulation, non-citizen voting, and mail-in ballot fraud are the most common alleged mechanisms of fraud — which we unfortunately expect to see after the 2026 midterm election.
